The 7th meeting of the 57th session of the Statistical Commission is called to order. Distinguished delegates, I understand that many participants are scheduled to take flights home this afternoon or evening. Let's do our best to complete our discussion and close the session by 1 PM by keeping our deliberations as concise as possible. However, if we are unable to finish all agenda items this morning, We may need to use the afternoon for another meeting to complete our discussions. Delegations intending to deliver statements are encouraged to send copies of those statements to estatements@un.org to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Distinguished delegates, the Commission will now begin its consideration of Agenda Item 6, entitled Program Questions, Statistics Division, under which it will receive an oral report by the Acting Director of the United Nations Statistics Division, Mr. Shantanu Mukherjee, concerning current activities, plans, and priorities of the Division.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished delegates. Good morning, everybody. Let me begin as a good national statistician should, with a preliminary estimate. So we have 96 countries in the room this year, 44 agencies and 5 non-governmental organizations. My team is sure these counts will go up by the time revised estimates come out, which is after 13th March. You have also read 36 official substantive documents, which were accompanied by 76 background documents. Surely that's some kind of record. For all of you. And between you, you've taken part in 81 side events. Those numbers are remarkable at any time, but this year, with budgetary and logistical constraints, even more so. But this fits in with what we saw during World Statistics Day last year— a major increase in awareness and engagement across the world when it comes to data and Statistics. Ladies and gentlemen, let me now talk a little bit about the program of the Statistics Division, which is closely related to the work of this Commission. We are always grateful for the additional resources we receive from you, whether financial or in-kind, and these are all the more vital at a time when regular resources are tight. I I'd like to take a moment to just acknowledge contributions from the following countries over the last year: China, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Norway, Saudi Arabia, and the UK. And also some of our institutional contributors: the European Commission, Eurostat, FAO, ILO, UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, UN Women, and the World Bank. Of course, going beyond this, we count on our collaborations with partner agencies in delivering our program. For example, the implementation of the SNA 2025 is proceeding in collaboration with our partners in the Intersecretariat Working Group, and much of our capacity development work is successful only because of the collaborations we have with the UN Regional Commissions as well as specialized agencies. Colleagues, over the past few days you've heard from us and read in our reports quite a bit about UNST's work over the last year. I hope what you've taken away is that despite some challenging times and staff transitions, UNST remains fully committed to supporting you and in advancing the causes of better data more representative statistics, and timely evidence for decision-making. As we look ahead, I would like to share with you some of our planned activities for the coming months. We do quite a lot, but— and this is more than just the tip of the iceberg, but maybe not that much more. But let me present it in terms of 3 strategic objectives. Our first objective is to strengthen foundations while being sure we can fully reflect the changes that are occurring around us. Under this, I will offer 3 items we work on. The first is that the adoption of the 2025 SNA along with the 2030 Population and Housing Census program last year gave all of us clear marching orders when it comes to implementation. We are proceeding to do so. For example, in the S&As, through establishing an implementation hub, supporting countries in developing their implementation plans, coordinating the support that's available, targeted— developing targeted guidance materials and other support. I also want to note that we will be able to offer hands-on support to countries through our newly recruited Interregional Advisor for Census, and hopefully through a similar position for the SNA as well. When it comes to this strategic objective, we are also anticipating an exciting year ahead towards setting new milestones: advancing the central framework for SPSS, finalizing new guidance towards updating the SEER central framework, and developing tools and methods to better capture the complex and consequential interactions between nature and people. And finally here in this list, we would also like to make it easier for ourselves and countries to move from isolated datasets to integrated systems, combining survey, administrative, geospatial, and citizen-generated data through common standards, compatible processes, and clear methods for linkage and interpretation. Within this range of work, I would also include AI readiness, both when it comes to our own data as well as supporting countries with guidance for their NSOs. Now, our second strategic objective— this is closing the gap. In economics, we sometimes talked about K-shaped processes where divergence between countries grows rather than narrowing. In UNSD, one of our objectives is to avoid the K when it comes to statistics and data. We do this through greater focus in meeting countries where they are at and supporting them in accelerating the development of capacity in different areas of statistical work. Again, let me just give 3 examples. The first is to note that this approach is cross-cutting for us. So whether it is the implementation of the SNA 2025 or 2030 census rounds, we would like to proceed on the basis of capacity needs assessments and express demand to better target our support. We will also continue to develop and roll out specialized products for countries. For example, the EBAS monitoring framework for the Small Island Developing States, and in related work, sustaining the imperative for developing long-term solutions to the production of demographic and health data, where we host and support the Intersecretariat Working Group on Household Surveys, and we feel we can support them in taking forward the work that commenced last India in the wake of abrupt funding cuts that paralyzed data collection in the poorest of countries. And of course, as the Commission grows, we would count on your support to help us ensure that new members, especially from the less developed parts of the world, are able to contribute fully to your important work. Perhaps not in all 43 of the expert groups at the same time,, but still in the ones that matter to them. My third strategic objective is to support and embrace global movements towards better data and policy. As a statistical community, we engage with policymakers and others who drive change in different fora. Here at UNST, our focus will be on the following: First, using SDG monitoring as a springboard for the future. The SDG Summit in 2027, the last before 2030, promises to be a unique moment to bring not just assessments of progress and shortfalls, but also what we have learned in terms of using statistics for global agendas. Our annual SDG reports, particularly the 2027 special edition, will put forward this knowledge. Curated with the support of all our partners and also the IAG SDG task team. Second, Beyond GDP. The Secretary-General's High-Level Group will be launching its report next month, and an initial presentation earlier this week at the General Assembly drew a lot of support and interest. Here also at the Commission, we heard about the resonance this agenda has in countries across the world and the range of approaches you are following to support it. I expect that UNST will be called upon to provide substantive support to this area of work, and we are ready to do so. And then, of course, in this category also falls the UN System Data Commons, an authoritative entry point for accessing the federated ecosystem of UN data with advancing cross-domain analytic capabilities that can help expand access and promote better use of data. We are fully committed to doing that along with many partner agencies, some who are in the room and some who are not. And of course, please mark your calendars for the UN World Data Forum, 9th to 12th November in Riyadh this year. Friends, I began by calling out the manifest recognition of the importance of our work in our countries and in all other areas we work in. I hope you see in our plans for the year ahead that here at UNST we are keenly aware of our responsibilities. You can count on us, and I'm sure that we too will be able to count on you, not just as trusted partners but also as UNCTE's advocates and stewards as we move ahead.

Thank you.
